title: The lotus on the rubbish heap (53–59)
hook: the scent of virtue travels against the wind; a lotus grows on a heap by the road

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bee, who takes the nectar and leaves the flower whole. Your line: the bee leaves the flower. Today, the last day of the flower chapter.
screen: `THE BEE — THE BEE LEAVES THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: A bakery on a cold morning sends the smell of bread half a block down the street. But only downwind. Walk upwind and there's nothing. Scent goes where the wind goes. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, once asked him about exactly this. Is there any scent, anywhere, that can travel against the wind? The answer closes the flower chapter.
screen: `BREAD, HALF A BLOCK AWAY.` → `ONLY IF YOU'RE DOWNWIND.` → `ANY SCENT AGAINST THE WIND?`

segments.voice: Verse fifty-four gives the answer. The scent of flowers doesn't travel against the wind, not even sandalwood or jasmine, “but the odour of good people travels even against the wind.” Goodness is the one fragrance that goes everywhere. People hear about a kind person in places the person has never been. Verse fifty-three sets it up: as many garlands can be made from a heap of flowers, so much good can be done by someone once they're born. Verses fifty-five to fifty-seven add that among all perfumes, sandal, lotus and the rest, the scent of virtue is the highest, and that Mara can't even find the path of those who live well. Then the chapter ends on a picture of its own. Verses fifty-eight and fifty-nine: “as on a heap of rubbish cast upon the highway the lily will grow full of sweet perfume and delight.” Müller wrote lily. The Pali says paduma: lotus. Picture a trash heap on the side of a road: broken pots, peelings, dust. And growing out of the refuse, a lotus, clean and still fragrant. So, the verse goes on, a disciple of the Buddha shines out by wisdom among people walking in darkness. The flower doesn't wait for a clean pond. Buddhist tradition takes the lotus as a picture of exactly this: rooted in the mud, rising out of it, unstained. So the flower chapter ends not in a garden, but beside the road, where a lot of real life happens.
screen: `A SCENT AGAINST THE WIND.` · `MANY GARLANDS FROM ONE HEAP.` · `MÜLLER'S LILY IS A LOTUS.` · `ROOTED IN THE MESS, UNSTAINED.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS ON THE HEAP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one rough place in your life: a tired street you walk down, a difficult job, a home messier than you'd like, a hard stretch of this year. Look there, gently, for one lotus that grew right out of it, like a neighbor who waves, a coworker who covers for you, a small courage you didn't know you had. Breathe with it, not denying the heap, just seeing the flower too.
Paduma. Lotus: goodness growing clean and fragrant out of a rubbish heap, its scent going even against the wind.
Your line: the lotus on the heap. Rooted in the mess, and still fragrant. Day one hundred seventy, done.

howItsDone: The lotus rising from mud is a Buddhist symbol seen in temple art and offerings, and teachers use the rubbish-heap verses to say that awakening can grow from ordinary, difficult life.

a lily that blooms only in a clean garden pond

fork.setup: Ananda asks the Buddha: is there any scent that travels against the wind? what's the answer?
options: yes: the scent of good people's virtue.
fork.reveal: flower scents go only with the wind; the fragrance of goodness goes in every direction.

original.note: Pali: lotus, the flower on the rubbish heap in verse fifty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: the verse says goodness belongs in clean, beautiful places.
what it means: goodness grows out of rough places, like a lotus from a trash heap by the road.
what a scholar hears: verse 58's 'sankaradhanasmim ujjhitasmim mahapathe, padumam tattha jayetha': a lotus born on a rubbish heap thrown by the highway; Müller's 'lily' is his rendering of padumam.
recall: verses you recite but don't live

notes: Check Müller's verses 54 and 58 against SBE 10 (British 'odour' kept inside quotation). Verse 58 begins 'As on a heap of rubbish'; confirm the quoted clause.
Ananda's question about a scent that travels against the wind: also in AN 3.79 (Gandha Sutta); confirm.
Verse 54 names sandalwood, tagara and mallika; the voice simplifies to 'sandalwood or jasmine'. Confirm 'jasmine' for mallika.
'Lotuses grow best from mud' is a common teaching image; kept general.
